title: Error Recovery with Fallbacks
story: Real systems don't just crash — they try alternatives. Your app connects to a primary database, but if it's down, it tries a backup. If the backup is down too, it tries a local cache. Only when all three fail does it finally give up and report the error.
why: Trying fallback operations with `match` and `if let` is the pattern behind retry logic, failover systems, and resilient architectures.
analogy: Error recovery is like trying to get into your house. You reach for your keys (primary) — not in your pocket. You check under the doormat (backup) — no spare key. You try the back door (cache) — it's unlocked! You go in. Only if all three are locked do you sit on the porch and call a locksmith. Each attempt is an independent operation that either succeeds or passes control to the next.
try_it: Change which operation succeeds (make A succeed, B and C fail; make B succeed; make all fail). Add a fourth operation D. Add a counter that tracks how many attempts were made. Use `match` instead of `if let` to capture and print which error each failed operation returned. Change the final error message to include all attempted errors.
tips: `if let Ok(val) = expr` is shorthand: 'if this is Ok, bind the value to val and run the block, otherwise skip it'
`result is Ok` tests the variant without extracting — use it when you only care about success vs failure
Fallback order matters — try the most desirable option first (fastest, cheapest, or best quality)
common_mistakes: Using `?` in a fallback chain — `let conn = connect_primary()?;` would return Err immediately, never trying the backup
Shadowing variables across attempts — `let result = connect_a(); let result = connect_b();` is fine since each shadows the previous
